# Potica Troubleshooting
URL: https://www.poticas.com/guides/potica-troubleshooting.html
==============================================================

potica s
Learn
Shop
Community
About Potica
Poticas.com › Guides › Troubleshooting
## Potica Troubleshooting : Every Failure Has a Cause
By Poticas.com · Updated July 2026
Cut the loaf, read the cross-section. The spiral tells you exactly what went wrong — and none of it is fatal.
Why did my potica crack or have gaps inside?
Gaps between the layers come from a loose roll, an over-proved second rise, or a filling too dry to bond to the dough. A cracked top means the tin was too small, the oven too hot, or the surface dried during proving. A doughy centre means underbaked — potica is done at about 90 °C internal.
## Quick Diagnosis Chart
Symptom Most likely cause Fix next time
Hollow gaps between spiral layers Loose roll, or over-proved in the tin Roll tighter; cap second prove at ~45 min
Top cracked open Tin too small, oven too hot, or skin dried during prove Bigger tin; check oven temp; cover during second prove
Filling leaked / burnt sugar on tin Runny filling or unsealed seam Warm honey gently, never hot; pinch the full seam length
Dense, doughy, or gummy centre Underbaked or under-proved; or sliced warm Bake to ~90 °C internal; prove fully; cool completely
Dry, crumbly slice Overbaked, or filling too dry Tent with foil at 30 min; don't skimp the filling liquid
Tore during rolling Gluten tight or dough under-proved Rest dough 5 min when it fights back; patch with wet fingers
## Gaps Between the Layers
The classic potica failure: you slice, and there are hollow tunnels where filling should meet dough. Three causes, in order of likelihood:
- The roll was loose. Air trapped between turns expands in the oven, then the structure collapses around it. Roll firmly — the cloth technique makes a tight roll much easier.
- Over-proved in the tin. During the second prove the dough inflates away from the filling; in the oven that exaggerated rise collapses into a gap, usually a crescent under the top crust. Keep the second prove to about 45 minutes.
- Filling too dry. A dry filling doesn't adhere to the dough, so the layers separate where they never bonded. Respect the recipe's honey, rum, and egg white — they are the glue.
## Cracked Top
A crack means internal pressure found a weak point. Either the tin was too small (the loaf had nowhere to grow but up and out), the oven ran hot (crust set before the inside finished expanding), or the surface dried into a rigid skin during the second prove — cover the tin loosely with a cloth while it proves. A hairline crack is cosmetic; a canyon is a message.
## Filling Leaked Out
Caramelised filling welded to the tin means either the filling was too liquid or the seam let go. Honey heated too far is the usual culprit for runny filling — warm it just to pourable. For the seam: leave the 4 cm bare strip when spreading, pinch the seam shut along its entire length, and bake seam-down (or seam-outward in a ring mould) so gravity works with you.
## Dense or Doughy Centre
Potica is dense by design, but it should never be gummy or raw at the core. Real causes:
- Underbaked. This loaf is a heat-sink. Trust a thermometer (about 90 °C in the deepest point) or a skewer, not the surface colour — the top browns long before the middle cooks. Loaf tins are more prone to this than ring moulds; the cone exists precisely for this reason .
- Under-proved dough bakes dense everywhere, not just centrally. The poke test prevents it.
- Sliced warm. A warm potica reads gummy even when perfectly baked. The crumb sets as it cools. Full cooling is part of the bake.
## Dry Potica
Overbaking is the obvious cause — tent with foil once the top is golden, and pull it at temperature rather than by the clock. The subtler cause is a mean filling: the ratio of nuts to honey/rum/egg-white exists to keep the interior moist for days. A skimped filling bakes into sawdust no matter how good the dough is. And note that potica dries from the cut face once opened — store it cut-side covered .
## The Consolation
A cracked, gapped, lopsided potica still tastes like potica. The filling does the work; the spiral is more forgiving than it looks. Diagnose, take the note for next time, and eat the evidence. If you want a second opinion on the cross-section, post it in the community — potica autopsies welcome.
## Frequently Asked Questions
Why did my potica separate from the filling?
Either the roll was loose (trapped air expands, then collapses into gaps), the shaped loaf over-proved in the tin (dough inflates away from the spiral), or the filling was too dry to bond to the dough. Tight roll, 45-minute second prove, full-moisture filling.
How do I know when potica is fully baked?
Internal temperature around 90 °C at the deepest point, or a skewer that comes out with no wet dough. Surface colour is misleading — the top browns long before the dense centre finishes.
Why is my potica gummy in the middle?
Underbaked, under-proved, or — most commonly — sliced while still warm. The crumb of an enriched loaf sets during cooling; even a perfect potica reads gummy if you cut it hot.
Can I fix a potica that cracked on top?
Not after the fact — but it is purely cosmetic. Next bake: larger tin, verify the oven temperature, and cover the loaf loosely during the second prove so the surface never dries into a rigid skin.

# Storing Potica
URL: https://www.poticas.com/guides/storing-potica.html
==============================================================

potica s
Learn

About Potica
Poticas.com › Guides › Storing Potica
## Storing Potica: It Gets Better on Day Two
By Poticas.com · Updated July 2026
One of the only pastries that rewards patience twice — once before the knife, and once overnight.
How long does potica last?
Wrapped well at room temperature, potica keeps about 5–7 days — and it genuinely improves on day two as the filling's moisture settles into the crumb. It freezes excellently for about 3 months, whole or by the slice. Avoid the refrigerator, which stales the crumb faster than the counter.
## The Day-Two Truth
Fresh-from-the-oven is the wrong day to judge a potica. Overnight, the moisture in the filling migrates into the surrounding crumb, flavours knit together, and the texture becomes what it was always supposed to be: dense, moist, sliceable into clean spirals. Bakers plan for this — bake Friday, serve Saturday. If your schedule allows a rest day, take it.
## Room Temperature: the Default
Potica is a keeper by construction — an enriched, dense loaf with a low-moisture nut filling. Wrapped well at cool room temperature it stays genuinely good for about 5–7 days , which is exactly why it became the celebration bread of farmhouses without refrigeration and survived steamship crossings to America.
- Whole loaf: wrap tightly in foil or plastic wrap, or keep in an airtight container, away from sunlight and the stove.
- Once cut: the cut face is where it dries. Press foil or wrap directly against the exposed spiral, then wrap the loaf. Slice from one end only.
- Slices for the week: cut as needed, not in advance — pre-sliced potica stales fastest of all.
## The Refrigerator Question
Generally: don't. Refrigeration accelerates staling in bread-type crumb — the fridge makes potica dry and firm faster than the counter does. The exceptions are practical: a very warm and humid kitchen, or a cream-cheese or fresh-cheese filling variant, which belongs refrigerated for safety. Classic walnut and poppy fillings are shelf-stable in the loaf for the week they will survive uneaten (they never survive the week).
## Freezing
Potica freezes exceptionally well — its density is an asset here.
- Whole or half loaves: cool completely, wrap tightly in plastic, then in foil (two layers is the difference between frozen and freezer-burnt). Good for about 3 months .
- By the slice: freeze slices on a tray, then bag them. Pull one at a time with coffee for the rest of winter — this is the connoisseur's move.
- Thawing: at room temperature, still wrapped, so condensation forms on the wrapper instead of the crumb. A few hours for slices, overnight for a loaf. A 10-minute refresh in a 150 °C oven revives the crust of a whole loaf.
## Gifting & Shipping
Potica's keeping quality is why it has always been a gifted food — and why diaspora families could mail loaves across the country to relatives, a tradition Iron Range and Cleveland bakeries turned into a mail-order business model that still runs today. Shipping your own: bake, cool fully (a warm loaf sweats inside wrapping), double-wrap, and ship early in the week so it never sits in a depot over a weekend. A well-wrapped potica arrives in better shape on day three than most pastries manage on day one.
### No time to bake one?
The shop lists trusted bakeries that ship traditional potica — plus the pantry for when you do bake.
Order Potica →
## Frequently Asked Questions
How long does potica last?
Wrapped well at room temperature, about 5–7 days — it is a dense, enriched loaf built to keep. Frozen, about 3 months. Once cut, protect the cut face directly with wrap or foil; that is where it dries first.
Should potica be refrigerated?
Usually no — refrigeration stales bread-type crumb faster than the counter. Refrigerate only in hot, humid conditions or if the filling contains fresh cheese or cream cheese.
Can you freeze potica?
Yes, and it freezes beautifully. Double-wrap (plastic, then foil) a fully cooled loaf or freeze individual slices on a tray first. Thaw at room temperature still wrapped, so condensation lands on the wrapper rather than the crumb.
Is potica better the next day?
Genuinely yes. Overnight, moisture from the filling migrates into the crumb and the flavours meld — bakers deliberately bake a day ahead. Day two is the pastry at its best.

# Tarragon Potica (Pehtranova Potica)
URL: https://www.poticas.com/guides/tarragon-potica.html
==============================================================

potica s
Learn
Shop
Community
About Potica
Poticas.com › Guides › Tarragon Potica
## Tarragon Potica: Pehtranova Potica
By Poticas.com · Updated July 2026
The one that surprises everyone — a sweet herb roll with no equivalent anywhere else in European pastry. Slovenians consider it among the most traditional of all.
What is tarragon potica (pehtranova potica)?
A traditional Slovenian potica filled with fresh tarragon creamed into butter, sugar, eggs, and sour cream — sweet with a gentle anise-like warmth. It is one of the five fillings approved for EU-protected Slovenska potica and a long-standing Easter bake, especially cherished around Novo mesto in Dolenjska. Fresh tarragon only; dried does not work.
## The One That Surprises Everyone
Most people outside Slovenia have never met a sweet herb pastry, and on paper the combination reads like a mistake. It is not. Tarragon — pehtran in Slovene — is one of the five fillings approved for the EU-protected "Slovenska potica" , alongside walnut, walnut with raisins, raisin, and tarragon with cottage cheese. In Slovenia, tarragon lives in the sweet kitchen: fresh, anise-scented, folded into sugar and butter and cream, it produces a flavour with no equivalent anywhere else in European baking.
## An Easter Tradition
Pehtranova potica — affectionately pehtranka — is a spring and Easter bake. Fresh tarragon comes up early, right on time for the Easter table, and the pale-green roll sits beside the ham and coloured eggs in many Slovenian households. It is a specialty especially cherished in the Dolenjska region around Novo mesto, where local bakers treat it as a point of pride, though you will find it across the country.
## The Filling
Two traditional styles exist, and both are legitimate:
- Butter-cream style: softened butter creamed with sugar, eggs, and sour cream, with finely chopped blanched tarragon folded through.
- Cottage-cheese style (s skuto): the tarragon folded into a sweetened curd/cottage-cheese filling — "tarragon with cottage cheese" is itself one of the five protected fillings. Common, beloved, and slightly moister.
For the butter-cream version, per one loaf of the standard dough :
- 80–100 g fresh tarragon leaves, stripped from their stems
- 150 g sugar
- 80 g butter, softened
- 2 eggs
- 100 ml sour cream
- Pinch of salt
## Method Notes
Blanch the tarragon leaves for 30 seconds in boiling water and plunge them straight into ice water — this sets the colour and softens the herb's raw edge. Squeeze dry and chop very fine, almost to a paste. Cream the butter and sugar, beat in the eggs one at a time, add the sour cream, fold in the tarragon, season with a pinch of salt.
The filling goes on pale green and looks improbable. Bake it anyway. Roll, prove, and bake exactly as for the walnut version — 175 °C, 50 minutes, rolled thin and cooled fully. The green softens to olive in the oven and the whole house smells like a Slovenian village kitchen in April.
This is not a first-timer's potica. Learn the dough and the roll on walnut; come back to tarragon when your hands know the motions.
## Fresh Tarragon Only
Dried tarragon produces a different and significantly lesser thing — dusty where it should be bright. If you cannot find fresh tarragon (look for French tarragon; buy generously, the leaves cook down), wait until you can. The herb is the pastry.
## Frequently Asked Questions
What does tarragon potica taste like?
Sweet first, then a gentle anise-like warmth from the fresh tarragon — closer to a fennel-scented cream than anything savory. It is unusual on the first bite and addictive by the third. Slovenians consider it a classic, not a novelty.
Can I use dried tarragon for pehtranova potica?
No — dried tarragon loses the bright anise aromatics that define the pastry and leaves only a dusty, faintly medicinal note. Fresh French tarragon is the ingredient. If you can't get it, bake a different filling and wait for spring.
Is tarragon potica traditional or a modern invention?
Fully traditional — tarragon is one of the five fillings approved in the EU "Slovenska potica" specification, and pehtranova potica is a long-standing Easter bake, especially cherished around Novo mesto in the Dolenjska region.
What is pehtranova potica s skuto?
The cottage-cheese variant: sweetened curd (skuta) filling with the chopped tarragon folded through. It combines two of the five protected fillings and bakes slightly moister than the butter-cream style.

# Poppy Seed Potica (Makova Potica)
URL: https://www.poticas.com/guides/poppy-seed-potica.html
==============================================================

potica s
Learn
Shop
Community
About Potica
Poticas.com › Guides › Poppy Seed Potica
## Poppy Seed Potica: Makova Potica
By Poticas.com · Updated July 2026
Darker, more fragrant, and arguably the most striking of all the variations — almost black inside, flecked with orange zest.
What is poppy seed potica (makova potica)?
The dark, fragrant sibling of the walnut roll: ground poppy seeds mixed with sugar, hot milk, butter, and orange zest, rolled inside the same enriched yeast dough. Called makovnjača in Croatia, where it anchors the Christmas table. The seeds must be ground — whole poppy seeds bake up gritty and nearly flavourless.
## The Dark Sibling
Slice a walnut potica and a poppy seed potica side by side and you get the two poles of Central European baking: gold spirals against near-black ones. The poppy filling is darker in flavour too — gently bitter, floral, deeply fragrant in a way walnut never quite reaches. Makova potica is among Slovenia's most traditional varieties — though note the narrow list protected by the 2021 EU "Slovenska potica" specification runs to walnut and tarragon fillings; poppy's kingdom is the broader tradition, and above all Croatia's Christmas table. Its partisans are the most loyal in the entire potica world.
## Whose Roll Is It?
Everyone's. In Slovenia, makova potica shares the holiday table with walnut. In Croatia the same roll is makovnjača — a fixture of Christmas, and in Slavonia a table without it is considered incomplete. Hungary bakes the poppy bejgli at Christmas; Poland has makowiec . The poppy branch of the rolled-pastry family tree may be its most international one ( the family tree, mapped ).
## You Must Grind the Seeds
The step everyone skips, and the reason so many home poppy rolls disappoint: whole poppy seeds are sealed capsules . Baked whole, they stay gritty and taste like almost nothing. Ground, they release their oils and become the dark, fragrant paste the pastry is named for.
Grind in a dedicated poppy/spice grinder, a clean burr coffee grinder, or a high-speed blender in short bursts, until the seeds look like coarse wet sand and clump slightly. (A food processor alone is usually too coarse for poppy — the seeds are tiny and slip the blade.) If you can only find pre-ground poppy, buy it from a busy Eastern European grocer and use it fast: ground poppy goes rancid quickly.
## The Filling
Per one loaf of the standard dough :
- 350 g poppy seeds, ground (see above)
- 120 g sugar
- 80 ml hot milk
- 40 g butter, melted
- 1 tsp vanilla
- Zest of one orange
- 2 tbsp rum (optional, but traditional)
Pour the hot milk and melted butter over the ground seeds, add everything else, and stir to a thick, spreadable paste. Too loose, add more ground seed; too stiff, a splash more warm milk. The orange zest is the signature — those bright flecks against the near-black filling.
## Method Notes
Everything else follows the walnut playbook: roll thin , spread generously (poppy filling cooks down more than walnut — do not be shy), roll tight, seal, prove 45 minutes, bake at 175 °C for about 50 minutes, and cool completely before slicing . Slice thin: poppy potica is intense, and a slim dark spiral next to a gold walnut one is the best-looking board in Central European baking.
## Frequently Asked Questions
Do I really have to grind poppy seeds for potica?
Yes. Whole poppy seeds are hard little capsules that bake up gritty and bland. Grinding ruptures them and releases the oils — that is where all the flavour lives. A spice grinder, burr grinder, or blender in bursts gets them to the coarse-wet-sand stage you need.
What is the difference between makova potica and makovnjača?
The same poppy seed roll wearing its Slovenian name (makova potica) and its Croatian name (makovnjača). Croatia leans on it at Christmas; Slovenia bakes it for holidays alongside the walnut version.
Why is my poppy seed filling bitter?
Either the seeds were stale (poppy goes rancid fast, especially pre-ground — buy fresh, store cold) or the filling lacks the sugar, milk, and zest that round poppy's natural gentle bitterness into fragrance.
Can I use canned poppy seed filling?
It works mechanically, but canned filling is mostly sugar syrup and runs sweeter, looser, and flatter than fresh-ground seeds with hot milk and orange zest. For the roll the pastry is named after, grind fresh.

## Pots & Pans: The Whole Potica Kitchen
Every tool the bake actually uses, from the potičnik to the flour-sack towel. Two tiers, honestly labeled: economy picks and hunted-down maker picks.
How the links work: ECONOMY buttons go to Amazon — they're affiliate links and I earn a small commission at no cost to you. WORTH THE HUNT buttons go to my sister site 5best2buy , which hunts down small American makers — the premium tier, and nobody pays to be there. Buy once, cry once; or buy economy and bake tonight. Both are honorable.
Jump to:
Bake & Shape · Roll & Work · Mix & Knead · Measure & Temp · Grind & Prep · Slice, Store & Gift · Keep & Clean · The Ingredient Shelf
## 🍩 Bake & Shape
The pan decides the bake — the potičnik guide explains why .
Tube / kugelhopf pan (the potičnik stand-in)
The closest thing to the traditional pan: ring shape, central cone, even bake.
Economy →
Bundt pan (simple pattern)
Works beautifully — pick plain flutes, not intricate ones, and grease everything.
Economy →
Angel food / two-piece tube pan
Plain walls release a heavy enriched loaf more forgivingly than any fluted pan.
Economy →
Loaf pan, 9×5 (the diaspora standard)
How most American potica has been baked for a century.
Economy →
Loaf pan set (bake two at once)
The classic recipe halves into two standard tins — one to keep, one to give.
Economy →
Mini loaf pans
Gift-size poticas — the church-sale format.
Economy →
Baking sheet set
For free-form coiled poticas and toasting the walnuts.
Economy →
Cooling rack
Cooling fully before slicing is a rule, not a suggestion — this is where it happens.
Economy →
## 🥖 Roll & Work
The roll is the skill — the rolling guide shows what these are for.
French tapered rolling pin
Feel and control for thin dough; the pin most bakers end up loyal to.
Economy →
Classic rolling pin with handles
Weight does the work on the first passes of a stiff dough.
Economy →
Rolling pin thickness rings
Rubber bands for consistency — a 3 mm guarantee on every pass.
Economy →
Pastry cloth (large)
The traditional surface — stops sticking and lifts the dough into the roll for you.
Economy →
Silicone pastry mat with measurements
The modern cloth — printed guides tell you when the rectangle hits 50×35 cm.
Economy →
Marble pastry board
Stays cool, resists sticking — the luxury the dough notices.
Economy →
Bench scraper (stainless)
Divides dough, lifts dough, cleans the counter — the most-used tool in bread baking.
Economy →
Flexible bowl scrapers
Gets every gram of filling out of the bowl and onto the dough.
Economy →
Pastry brush set
Egg wash on, excess flour off.
Economy →
## 🌀 Mix & Knead
What "smooth and elastic" takes — the dough guide has the windowpane test.
Stand mixer with dough hook
Ten minutes of hand-kneading becomes six of supervision.
Economy →
Hand mixer
For the filling: creaming butter, whipping the egg whites to stiff peaks.
Economy →
Bread machine (dough cycle)
Heresy? Maybe. But its dough cycle kneads and proves enriched dough flawlessly while you grind walnuts.
Economy →
Danish dough whisk
Brings shaggy dough together faster than a spoon, cleaner than hands.
Economy →
Stainless mixing bowl set
Dough in the big one, filling in the middle one, egg whites in the small one.
Economy →
Glass mixing bowls with lids
Watch the dough double instead of guessing.
Economy →
Dough rising bucket (marked)
Volume markings turn "has it doubled?" into a reading, not a debate.
Economy →
Wooden spoon set
The filling wants slow, warm stirring. Grandmother technology, unimproved since 1575.
Economy →
Silicone spatula set
Folding stiff egg whites into walnut filling without deflating them.
Economy →
## 🌡️ Measure & Temp
Potica is done at ~90 °C inside, and yeast dies above ~45 °C — numbers beat vibes.
Digital kitchen scale (grams)
The single most important tool on this page. 500 g of flour is not "about 4 cups."
Economy →
Instant-read thermometer
Milk at 37 °C, loaf at 90 °C — ends both arguments instantly.
Economy →
Oven thermometer
Most home ovens lie by 10–20 degrees. A cracked top is often just a hot oven.
Economy →
Measuring spoons (narrow)
For the yeast, salt, cinnamon, and clove — narrow ones fit spice jars.
Economy →
Measuring cups (liquid)
Warm milk by the millilitre.
Economy →
Folding bread proofer
A warm, humidity-controlled box — the Iron Range grandmothers heated the whole house; this heats one cubic foot.
Economy →
## ⚙️ Grind & Prep
Texture is everything — walnuts and poppy seeds each have a guide.
Hand-crank nut grinder / mill
The traditional tool and still the best: shears the nut dry instead of crushing it oily.
Economy →
Rotary drum grater
Same shearing action, smaller footprint, excellent budget stand-in.
Economy →
Food processor
Works if you pulse in batches — the guide explains the walnut-butter trap.
Economy →
Spice / poppy seed grinder
Whole poppy seeds taste like almost nothing — this is the makova potica unlock.
Economy →
Microplane zester
Lemon zest in the dough, orange zest in the poppy filling.
Economy →
## 🔪 Slice, Store & Gift
Day two is the best day — the storing guide — and potica has always been a gifted food.
Serrated bread knife
Clean spiral slices instead of compressed smears.
Economy →
Bread slicing guide
Even thin slices, sixteen out of sixteen.
Economy →
Parchment paper
Lines the tin, wraps the gift.
Economy →
Bread box / storage container
Room temperature, wrapped, up to a week — never the refrigerator.
Economy →
Bread gift bags
The unspoken rule: if you bring a potica, you made it. Bag it like you mean it.
Economy →
Cake boards
A sturdy base for gifting or shipping a whole loaf.
Economy →
Flour sifter / sugar duster
The optional snowfall of powdered sugar on the finished spiral.
Economy →
## 🧽 Keep & Clean
The unglamorous half of every great bake.
Flour sack towels
Cover the proving bowl, line the basket — and in a pinch, they ARE the rolling cloth.
Economy →
Airtight flour containers
Bulk flour stays fresh; bulk walnuts live in the freezer instead.
Economy →
Oven mitts (long)
A 2 kg loaf in a metal tube pan holds heat like a engine block.
Economy →
Apron
Flour reaches places physics cannot explain.
Economy →
Pan scraper set
Baked-on honey filling surrenders to plastic scrapers, not steel wool.
Economy →
Dish brush set
The bundt pan's flutes demand a brush with opinions.
Economy →
## 🌾 The Ingredient Shelf
The gold buttons go to 5best2buy's live maker shelves — the sourcing map for this pastry is now complete.
Walnuts (bulk)
500 g per loaf — taste before you commit . Freezer-store.
Economy → Worth The Hunt →
Raw honey
Binds and sweetens the classic filling — a varietal honey earns its keep here.
Economy → Worth The Hunt →
Bread flour
Higher protein = the strength to roll thin without tearing.
Economy → Worth The Hunt →
Poppy seeds (bulk)
For makova potica — buy fresh, grind them, always.
Economy →
Instant yeast
A pound of SAF costs what six sachets do and keeps for a year in the freezer.
Economy →
Raisins (unsulphured)
For the walnut-raisin filling — soak them in the rum first.
Economy → Worth The Hunt →
Ceylon cinnamon
Softer and more floral than the grocery-jar cassia.
Economy → Worth The Hunt →
Vanilla extract
A teaspoon in the poppy filling; real extract, not flavoring.
Economy → Worth The Hunt →
Fine sea salt
Cleaner than iodized in an enriched dough.
Economy → Worth The Hunt →
European-style butter
Higher fat, gently tangy — richer dough, more tender crumb.
Economy → Worth The Hunt →
Pasture-raised eggs
Yolks in the dough and filling, whipped whites for lift — deeper gold from better birds.
Worth The Hunt →
Unrefined cane sugar
A caramel note in the dough and filling that white sugar can't reach.
Economy → Worth The Hunt →
Unwaxed lemons & specialty citrus
The zest is in every classic filling — unwaxed matters when the peel is the ingredient.
Worth The Hunt →
The full sourcing edition
The whole recipe with a hunted maker beside every ingredient that matters — on the sister site.

## The Potica Notebook
Short, dated notes from the world of potica — history, technique, bakeries, and traditions. A new entry every few days.
6 July 2026
## 1689: the first full description
Janez Vajkard Valvasor's encyclopedic Glory of the Duchy of Carniola (1689) gave the first detailed description of potica — thin dough coated with honey and walnuts, tightly rolled — a recipe that mirrors the modern walnut potica almost exactly, three and a half centuries later. More →
4 July 2026
## Potica's first appearance in print was a complaint
The earliest written record of potica comes from Primož Trubar's catechism writings of 1575 and 1577 — the reformer who gave Slovenian its first printed book also disapproved, in print, of women offering potice as votive gifts. The pastry was already so embedded in folk life that it made it into theology. More →
4 July 2026
## Only five fillings are legally 'Slovenska potica'
Under EU Regulation 2021/656, a potica sold as protected "Slovenska potica" may contain exactly five fillings: walnut, walnut with raisins, raisin, tarragon, or tarragon with cottage cheese. Everything else is delicious — but it isn't the protected article. The full specification →
Want the long-form version? Start with About Potica or the Baker's Guides .

About Potica
## About This Site
One person, one pastry, no committee.
I'm Vincent Gonzalez , and Poticas.com is my site — researched, written, and maintained by me. It started the way most potica stories start: with a grandmother, a floured cloth, and a recipe that lived in her hands. This site exists so that what she and a hundred thousand bakers like her knew doesn't depend on memory alone.
What's here: the referenced history of potica , baker's guides for actually making it, where to buy the real thing , and a community page where the feed contains only real posts by real people — nothing on this site is staged, seeded, or invented, and every historical claim traces to a source I've personally read. Some shop links earn me a small commission (they're labeled); the recommendations that earn me nothing are labeled too, because some of the best sources aren't affiliates.
I also contribute potica and povitica history to Wikipedia, and I'm preparing a research paper on the pastry's American record. If you spot something wrong here, tell me in the community — I fix things fast and thank you sincerely.
Every spiral holds a story. This one's mine.
